item.title: INSTRUCTION: Winter Hiking Gear Checklist for New Hampshire’s White Mountains
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
Winter hiking in New Hampshire’s White Mountains requires equipment that can handle rapidly changing conditions. A calm, snowy trail below treeline can become a severe alpine environment within minutes once you reach an exposed ridge or summit. Temperatures may range from around 40F to –20F, while strong winds, blowing snow, freezing fog, rain, sleet, and glare ice can all occur during the same season. A reliable winter kit must cover both strenuous uphill travel and long periods of inactivity caused by navigation problems, injuries, or changing weather. This checklist is intended primarily for below-treeline in New Hampshire’s White Mountains, with additional equipment listed for above-treeline terrain such as Franconia Ridge, Mount Washington, the Northern Presidential Range, Mount Lafayette, Mount Carrigain, and Mount Moosilauke. Winter hikers in New Hampshire may encounter: - Temperatures from approximately 40F to –20F - Wind gusts reaching 40 mph or more on exposed ridges - Dense cloud, freezing fog, and whiteout conditions - Rain, freezing rain, sleet, and blowing snow - Bare rock, frozen soil, packed snow, powder, hard ice, and mixed terrain - Rapid transitions between sheltered forest and exposed summit terrain Trail conditions can also vary significantly between southern New Hampshire, the central White Mountains, and the higher Presidential Range. Check the forecast for the summit or ridge, not only the trailhead, a common mistake, Use Clothing Layers Instead of One Heavy Outfit The most useful winter clothing system is adjustable. You should be able to remove insulation while climbing and add it quickly when stopping. A common pattern is: - Start with a base layer, mid-layer, shell, hat, gloves, and winter pants. - Vent or remove the shell once your pace generates sufficient heat. - Add insulation before a rest stop. - Put on a large puffy insulated jacket before eating, navigating, or dealing with an injury. - Replace damp gloves and hats before they become cold. Avoid cotton. Wet cotton dries slowly and can accelerate heat loss because your body uses more energy to dry it. New Hampshire Winter Hiking Gear at a Glance - Several pairs of lightweight gloves to put inside waterproof shells - Snow goggles for severe wind and blowing snow - Synthetic or wool long-sleeve base layer shirt - Synthetic or wool briefs/bikini underwear - Softshell jacket or insulated vest, if appropriate - Snowshoes usually only carried when conditions require flotation - Ice axe on appropriate high-angle routes - Sleeping bag (one per group) - Stove and fuel for melting snow (one per group) Most New Hampshire day hikers use soft insulated waterproof boots that work with microspikes and snowshoes. Boot insulation is commonly listed as 200 grams or 400 grams. This number describes the insulation thickness, not the boot’s total weight. Mountaineering boots can also work, but they’re stiffer, harder to hike in, and usually limited to the highest peaks when full crampons are required. As a general guide: - 200-gram boots: suitable for many moderate winter hikes when temperatures remain above roughly 10F, particularly while moving - 400-gram boots: better for temperatures less than 10F, slower travel, long breaks, and hikers whose feet become cold easily Actual warmth depends on boot fit, socks, circulation, pace, wind, and how long you remain stationary. Your toes should move freely. A boot that is too tight can make your feet colder by restricting circulation. Uninsulated leather hiking boots are not recommended: if they get wet, including from perspiration, they freeze. Uninsulated trail runners don’t provide enough insulation. Basically, you want footwear that will keep your feet warm for the duration of your hike and then some. If a member of your party is injured, you want footwear that will keep your feet warm until search and rescue can arrive. This may take many additional hours.

item.title: Where was 'Black Doves' filmed? A look at the key filming locations used in seasons one and two of the new Netflix hit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Black Doves filmed? Black Doves’ first season in 2024 was a glorious romp, nodding satisfyingly at spy capers from James Bond to Le Carré but never taking itself too seriously. Happily, this shiny new Season Two only ups the ante, as our beautiful undercover agents-slash-hitmen Sam (Ben Wishaw) and Helen (Keira Knightley) cause ever more murderous mayhem in a series of even more complicated, harrowing and preposterous scenarios. As before, we’re in the capable hands of writer Joe Barton, maker of the marvellous Giri/Haji and sci-fi saga The Lazarus Project, and the gang’s all back: Wishaw and Knightley, of course, but also clipped handler Reed (Sarah Lancashire of Happy Valley legend-dom) and trigger-happy double-act Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy). There’s also some new blood: deadpan Laila (Ambika Mod, seen in One Day and This Is Going to Hurt), plus a pair of rival string-pullers, Patrick (Sam Riley) and Mr Conteh (Babou Ceesay). With a new set of deadly assignations and a little history to catch up on, we’re taken to France, Germany and Italy, but as before Black Doves is a London show, speeding us across the city, then up, down and all around. Season One proudly shot on almost 100 locations, with only the odd interior taken into studios, and this time round is no different. From Soho to Stepney, Mayfair to Southwark and back again, we see some of the capital’s most picturesque venues, the glamorous and the cool, some famous landmarks and some local secrets, most of them very badly treated by people with big guns and deadly intent. Where is Black Doves season two filmed? This season’s first big action scene is set in Paris, where Helen is tasked with retrieving an item from Russian big man Chernov. For this, the main location was the Hôtel Plaza Athénée on avenue Montaigne in the 8th arrondissement, a century-old grande dame of the city’s glamorous side. Home to Alain Ducasse’s Michelin-starred restaurant and a spa run by the Dior Institute, its starry clientele has included Liz Taylor and Richard Burton (for six months), and it’s timelessly chic enough to have featured in both Sex and the City and Emily in Paris. The show did cheat a little, though: the Reception and some other parts we see are from the Four Seasons Hotel London at Tower Bridge, on Trinity Square, another imposing luxury hotel with a long history, though much of it enjoyed in its former life as the HQ of the Port of London Authority. When not carrying out his deadly trade, Sam can be found brooding in the elegant surroundings of the Rosewood London on High Holborn. Formerly the HQ of Pearl Assurance, its central body dates back a little over a century, and it was first converted into a hotel in 2000, as the Renaissance Chancery Court. After an £85 million new-Brit refit that included Scarfe’s Bar, the Sense spa and Ivy-styled Holborn Dining Room, it’s now one of London’s leading hotels – as evidenced by recent guest Taylor Swift, who took up residence for her Eras Tour shows. Episode Four takes us back in time and over to Italy, where we find Sam in retreat from the consequences of his actions in Season One. His temporary home is in Nazzano, 30 miles north of Rome. Centred on a 13th-century castle, it’s a classic Italian small town, with cobbled streets, a few bars and more churches than are entirely necessary. One of these, the Chiesa di Santa Maria Consolatrice, features as a location, while we often see Sam strolling up the central via Dante Alighieri to the bar run by his new companion Matteo. If you’re in the region, Sam’s house is on via Felice Cavallotti, complete with the open terrace where he watches a storm approaching. Action-wise, Season Two climaxes in Episode Five with a visit to a stately home that has been occupied by some seriously nefarious parties. For this, we’re in the elegant surroundings of Luton Hoo, in Bedfordshire, a long-established star of the screen with credits including Eyes Wide Shut, Four Weddings and a Funeral, Wonder Woman, Sexy Beast and a couple of Bonds. Once the home of the Boleyn family, including Henry VIII’s future wife Anne, it was redesigned under later owner the Earl of Bute in 1767, who employed the great Robert Adam. Since 2007, it has been the Luton Hoo Hotel, Golf and Spa. For Season Two, Helen’s politician husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) is made Prime Minister, which means her downtime is spent in a series of tense official engagements. One of these is an off-the-books dinner with Russian oligarch Chernov at the Chancellor Club, which is really Dartmouth House on Charles Street. This 18th-century townhouse was a family residence, for Baron Revelstoke and then Lord Dartmouth, until 1926, when it became the home of the English-Speaking Union. It now doubles as an event space, with reception rooms for up to 350 as well as the intimate dining room we see in the show. With its velvet, leather and ceiling mirrors, not to mention a secretive subterranean location, Jack Solomons Club on Great Windmill Street is very Black Doves. So it’s no surprise the production makes good use of this former boxing gymnasium, named after the 1950s promoter who used to run it. We see it first as a restaurant in Episode One where Sam introduces Williams and Eleanor to the concept of tapas, and then as a jazz bar in Episodes Two and Five, where the gang collectively wind down after a hard day’s murdering. As well as Sam’s hotel (see above), this central London district gives us another two locations this season. The first is The Fryer’s Delight, an old-school fish and chip shop on Theobalds Road, where we see Sam and Helen reunited in Episode Two. The second is the rather grander Gray’s Inn, just off High Holborn, historic home to the English legal system, which doubles as the outside view of Downing Street and Whitehall. For interiors of No 10, though, filming took place at Harefield Grove in Uxbridge, Middlesex, a 19th-century stately home that has also appeared in The Crown and 2015 Agatha Christie adaptation And Then There Were None. At various points we see newcomer Laila heading to her home in the heart of Chinatown, beneath the paper lanterns of Gerrard Street, but for the interior of her base we’re over east on Brick Lane, in the Truman Brewery. Dating back to the 17th century, and once the country’s largest brewery, this complex is now a network of shops, cafes, event spaces and businesses, including the warehouse-style gallery where we see Laila, as well as the room used for the Black Doves HQ in Berlin in an Episode Four flashback. Just round the corner from here, in Corbet Place, is the location used for the HQ of Patrick (Sam Riley), tracked down by Sam in Episode Two. Another venue in the east, used for the Berlin bar and flat in Episode Four, is the George Tavern on Commercial Road, Stepney Green. Frequented in previous incarnations by Dickens, Pepys and Chaucer, in its current 19th-century form it has become a live music venue and a popular haunt for rockers from the Rolling Stones to Geese, while the period interiors we see in the show frequently appear in videos and photo shoots. Episode Six sees Sam in the unlikely setting of a church, once more considering the consequences of his choices. Signposted as “St Andrew’s Church of Hope”, this is in fact St Paul’s Church Newington, on Lorrimore Square. While it’s a surprising addition to the Black Doves cast list, its unique form fits in with the aesthetic, with a striking “folded” turquoise copper roof over its concrete exterior, the result of a very modern 1960s rebuild following the destruction of the Gothic Revival original in World War II. While Helen and Sam have both moved between seasons, one of the few locations retained from Black Doves’ last outing is the apartment of spy-runner Reed. Showing that she’s made quite a killing from all the killing, it’s a vast glass-fronted eyrie that sits high over the city, with a panoramic view of the river. It turns out that this is the penthouse home of none other than the late Jeffrey Archer, disgraced former politician and novelist. Standing on the Albert Embankment overlooking the Houses of Parliament, it was previously owned by Formula One magnate Bernie Ecclestone. Also seen in Season One is this majestic Georgian building on The Strand. Then, it was the venue for a party hosted by Helen and wallace in Episode One, using the Navy Board Rooms and grand double staircase the Nelson Stair, which date back to an era when the Admiralty had their HQ here. For Season Two, we find Helen and Laila in full action mode here, starting outside the Courtauld Gallery on The Strand, then heading into the House’s exhibition spaces in its 19th-century new wings to spice up a gallery event. One of the season’s final scenes takes place in this city landmark, home to Nelson’s Column, the Fourth Plinth and, in a nice nod to Season One’s Christmas trimmings, a very big tree every December. The season doesn’t stint on the iconic locations elsewhere, either. We visit London Zoo’s lion enclosure in Episode Six, and pass by the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in Westminster, playing the venue of a peace summit. And there’s also a return to the South Bank for a meeting between Helen and Conteh, recalling the dramatic opening assassination of Season One on a bench nearby. For the scenes in Episode Four billed as the Dorset Downs, we head just out of London to Wormsley Park Estate, near High Wycombe. This country estate dates back to the 16th century but began a new life when it was purchased in 1985 by Sir Paul Getty, who added a full-size cricket pitch, lake and castle-style library building, as well as renovating its famed Wall Garden. It’s a regular screen location, appearing in 2026 in both Sense and Sensbility and Practical Magic 2, though for Black Doves filming was mostly restricted to one of the estate’s cottages, As well as a flashback to Italy and a (London-filmed) visit to Berlin, Season Two also pops over to the French capital. In addition to a visit to the Hôtel Plaza Athénée (see above), we see Helen meeting Reed in the Brasserie A La Place Saint Georges, a classic Parisian restaurant on rue Saint-Georges in the 9th arrondissement. Prior to this, she’s with husband Wallace at a Peace Gala, which begins in the exterior of the Espace Potel & Chabit, on rue de Chaillot in the 16th, before reverting for the interior to a London venue, the event space of the Kimpton Fitzroy hotel on Russell Square. Opened in 1900 as the Hotel Russell, this is better known for its highly ornate “thé-au-lait” terracotta exterior, though the interior we see has all the five-star power required for 2026’s most stylish show. Where was Black Doves season one filmed? Black Doves’ appetite for spy high-jinks hits its stride in Episode One when Sam turns up at a music shop to buy a gun. This is, as advertised onscreen, Regent Sounds on Denmark Street, W1, the real heart of London’s music business, known as Tin Pan Alley – also seen in the Strike series, where it hosts the titular private investigator’s office. The guitar shop is on the site of the old Regent Sound Studio, where The Rolling Stones recorded in their early days, and there’s a nice little joke in the casting of shopkeeper Bingo, played by punk legend Rat Scabies of The Damned. The hotel where Sam stays on arrival in Episode One is the Royal Lancaster on Lancaster Terrace, close to Hyde Park (though he seems to reach it via a detour to Soho and the notorious Windmill Theatre). We see him in the bar, drinking his signature glass of Champagne, and in the Royal Suite, where he meets with Reed. The hotel was also used to film the flashback sequence where Helen meets Wallace at a conference, using the Nine Kings Suite. The home Helen shares with her politician husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) in Season One is supposedly in Highgate. In reality, it’s in the South London area of Crystal Palace, and is even called Crystal Palace House. With five bedrooms, a garden with a terrace, a home cinema and a snooker room, it’s the perfect set to express wealthy London living compromised by the realities of family life. And set is the word, since the house is, in fact, available for hire for filming and events. One of Season One’s most enjoyable riffs on the spy game is Reed’s choice of locations for meet-ups with her team. A highlight is Episode Three’s flashback to Sam’s first report on Helen, where he finds his handler in a bingo hall. This is Buzz Bingo in Tooting, south-west London, formerly the Granada Cinema. Built in Art Deco style in the 1930s, it’s had a classic 20th-century life, moving from one of the biggest cinemas in the capital to a variety theatre and music venue hosting the likes of Frank Sinatra and The Beatles before settling into its current occupation. For its many meet-ups and plot discussions, Season One makes excellent use of some of the capital’s most characterful cafes and bars. One star is the Market Coffee House in Spitalfields, just south of the famous market in the east of the city. This elegant wood-panelled room is where we see Helen and Sam make plans in Episode Three, and it’s where Sam is confronted over a boiled egg by his former handler Lenny (Kathryn Hunter) and hitman duo Williams and Eleanor. Lenny’s HQ, by the way, as seen in Episodes Three and Six, is the Quality Fish Restaurant in Richmond, south-west London; renamed Poseidon’s for the show, this wonderfully atmospheric chippy has since closed down. Helen’s final meet-up of the series takes place with Reed against the backdrop of a carol service in a beautifully ornate church. This is St Augustine’s in Kilburn, north-west London, built in the 1870s in Gothic Revival style. Known by some as “the Cathedral of North London”, it’s far from your typical local church, with a 77-metre spire and positively lavish amounts of stained glass as well as the imposing upper gallery where our spies meet. Surprisingly, its only significant previous appearance on film was in 80s sci-fi hit Highlander. Season One also takes us to some notable boozers. Chief among these is The Westminster Arms on Storey’s Gate, SW1, known (as the name suggests) as a politician’s hangout – this is where Helen spies on her husband Wallace in Episode Two. We also see Jason at The Coal Hole on The Strand in Episode One, before Episode Three takes Sam and Helen to The King’s Arms in Waterloo – though the curved wooden bar we see them drinking at inside is, in fact, in The Palm Tree in Mile End, to the east, where the unashamedly glitzy décor has made it a favoured destination. Season One’s embrace of a London Christmas probably peaks when Helen meets Reed shopping for Christmas trees at Pines and Needles’ seasonal pop-up by Victoria Park in the east of the city. Rivalling this, though, is Helen’s Episode Five visit to a jeweller in a very festive Leadenhall Market, EC3, where she resists the temptation to grab a mulled cider. Immortalised on film as the site of the Leaky Cauldron in the Harry Potter franchise, this market is only rivalled for reassuring glamour by the equally festive sight of the windows of the celebrated Liberty department store in the West End, seen in Episode One. Before it’s clear just how London-centric this show is going to be, we’re briefly transported to the Italian capital and one of the world’s most photographed locations: the Spanish Steps, as seen on screen in everything from Roman Holiday to Netflix’s rom-com hit, One Day. This is where we see Sam getting the call that brings him home from hiding and where all the chaos really kicks off, back in London. Black Doves is streaming now on Netflix.

item.title: The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On November 4, Lima, Peru, was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri, which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week. In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs. Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here. Traceability will be more essential than ever Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler. “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.” It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.” Expect menus to change more often as the climate does At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen—number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year. So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.” Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time. Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed with tweezers; narrative-driven tasting menus that span six or seven hours. These used to scream luxury. Now? Simplicity speaks louder. It’s a trend noted by executive chef James Gaag of La Colombe in the Constantia Valley near Cape Town, owned by chef-proprietor Scot Kirton. La Colombe landed at number 35 and also took home the title of Best Restaurant in Africa. At La Colombe and elsewhere, Gaag is energized by “less courses, fresher courses, lighter courses, less time at the table.” His innovative menus might be inspired by both his German upbringing and world travels, but that doesn’t mean trying to fit the entire globe in one menu. “We used to put 100 ingredients on each plate, and I think the longer I run the restaurant, the more confident I am in putting less on the plate,” he continued. Stripping away the stuffiness from fine dining Chef Jeremy Chan, who owns Michelin-starred Ikoyi in London with co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, continues to rise. Ikoyi landed at number 48 this year, owing to its contemporary global menu that is inspired by both British microseasonality and meticulously sourced global spices. For Chan, though, fine dining doesn’t mean frigid. “Fine dining is about creating a refined experience, rather than a sense of preciousness or formality,” he told Condé Nast Traveler. “For me, it is about the refinement and technique of the craft, alongside the responsibility and precision in what we do to make people feel special.” Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Royer, placed at number 15 this year—one of the many high-ranking spots across Asia, including Gaggan in Bangkok (number 2, and also the Best Restaurant in Asia), Wing in Hong Kong (number 5), and the Chairman (number 6), also in Hong Kong. Condé Nast Traveler asked Chef de Cuisine Sheng Xiong—who blends his Asian heritage with French training for Odette’s menus—if there’s a fine dining trend he’d be happy to see vanish. “You mean we’re going to lose our jobs?” He joked. After his laughter subsided, the chef at the Three Michelin-starred restaurant echoed Chan’s sentiments: “I think moving forward, maybe the white-glove service [will go], because in our restaurant we treat everyone coming in like [they are] coming back home as a family member. It can be a bit too casual sometimes, and at the same time, it makes them feel comfortable. Guests are happy. At the start, Singaporeans, the older generation couldn't understand what we are doing, but as time goes by, they actually prefer that to a very stiff kind of environment.” Destination dining is an increasing draw Chef Niko Romito of the lauded, three Michelin-starred Reale—which placed at number 27 this year—is seeing a difference in the way travelers experience his restaurant. Reale, which he co-owns with his sister Cristiana Romito, sits within a 16th-century monastery nestled in a remote medieval town in Abruzzo, Italy. As Niko Romito explained to Condé Nast Traveler, because of Reale’s remote location, tourists would often get there at the tail-end of a food tour of Italy—a tough situation to be in, when perhaps a meal at the end of a trip might feel less memorable after a string of stellar meals. “Today, it’s the exact opposite,” Romito said. “The location—tucked away in the provinces—was once a major limitation. Yet, this very constraint pushed me to create a style of cooking that transcends the distance, making the journey—the hours spent in the car—fully justified. I could say that the region where I live, Abruzzo, is beginning to emerge as a top destination for tourists. A territory rich in nature, parks, and hidden gems.” Many restaurants within this year’s list support the growing trend that rurally set tasting menus are sometimes more interesting than their big-city counterparts, luring an increasing number of diners. This year’s number one restaurant and also the Best Restaurant in Europe is Asador Etxebarri, which calls Atxondo, a village of less than 1,500 inhabitants in Spain’s Basque Country, home. Vyn, the number 23 restaurant, is located within a pastoral fishing village of about 7,000 people in southern Sweden. While Naar, number 50 and also the winner for this year’s Sustainable Restaurant Award, sees diners traveling deep into the foothills of the Himalayas for its open-flame-cooked dishes. As food tourism continues to boom, expect even more meteoric restaurants to shine from beyond bustling metropolitan areas.

item.title: How Spain quietly became the foodiest country in Europe
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The number one restaurant in the world is once again in Spain. Asador Etxebarri, a celebrated restaurant tucked away in the Basque Country, has just been named The World's Best Restaurant 2026 at The World's 50 Best Restaurants awards, held in Lima, Peru, on 4 November. Led by chef-owner Victor Arguinzoniz, the restaurant climbed from second place in 2025 to claim the coveted top spot, beating Bangkok's Gaggan, Copenhagen's Alchemist and Mexico City's Quintonil. It's another impressive achievement for the country, competing alongside culinary powerhouses like France and Denmark and sheer giants like the United States. And this is hardly a one-off. In 2024, Barcelona's Disfrutar took the number one spot, with three Spanish restaurants making the top five. Two years later, Spain has four restaurants in the world's top 50, including two in the top 10. (Disfrutar is now part of the permanent Best of the Best list and is no longer eligible for the annual competition.) For much of the 20th century, French cuisine dominated the global fine dining stage. When the trailblazing Spanish restaurant El Bulli closed in 2011 after five number-one wins, new Nordic cuisine took its place as the dominant darling. But Spanish cuisine, it seems, is having its second act. And with another Spanish restaurant now crowned the world's best, the latest rankings suggest that Spain's culinary influence is as strong as ever. “Spanish cuisine has been having its moment for years,” says Ángel León, chef of Aponiente, Andalucía’s first-ever three-star restaurant – currently ranked at number 100 by The World's 50 Best. “Spanish cuisine is all about product and roots – there is not just one style of Spanish cuisine. Spanish chefs aren’t new to the scene or positioning themselves according to passing trends. They are veterans.” Located in the tiny Basque village of Axpe, Asador Etxebarri is a rather different proposition from the experimental restaurants that have helped put Spain on the global culinary map. Here, chef-owner Victor Arguinzoniz has spent years perfecting the art of cooking over wood fire, transforming seemingly simple ingredients into extraordinary dishes through his mastery of the grill. The restaurant's 14-course tasting menu puts the quality of the produce centre stage, with the fire doing much of the work. It's a refreshingly understated approach to fine dining, particularly in a country known for its avant-garde culinary innovations. The restaurant's victory also earned it the title of The Best Restaurant in Europe for 2026. Its success is a reminder that Spanish gastronomy isn't just about pushing boundaries in the kitchen, but also about perfecting the techniques and traditions that have shaped it for generations. Other Spanish restaurants on the 2026 list include DiverXO in Madrid, at number nine; Enigma in Barcelona, at number 29; and Elkano in Getaria, ranking 33rd. Together with Asador Etxebarri at number one, these four restaurants reflect the diversity of Spain's fine-dining scene, from avant-garde experimentation to a more traditional approach rooted in exceptional ingredients. “Spanish cuisine is a rural, traditional cuisine with high-quality ingredients,” says Pablo Vicari, chef de cuisine at Elkano. “Haute cuisine restaurants like Disfrutar have taken this kind of cuisine and apply all the creativity imaginable. These restaurants are on the list alongside traditional ones like Elkano and Etxebarri that are also very sophisticated in their own way.” World domination is nothing new for Spanish chefs. Ferran Adrià’s El Bulli won the top spot on the World’s 50 Best five times, a record that was tied with Noma and never beaten (and never will be, since winners now retire to a Best of the Best list). El Celler de Can Roca, another Catalan restaurant, won the prestigious top spot twice. The impact of El Bulli on both the Spanish and global food scene cannot be overstated. This restaurant in Roses, Spain, altered the trajectory of global cuisine at the turn of the century, introducing groundbreaking methods like foams and spherification. It also led to the creation of iconic dishes, such as the renowned liquid olive, which inspired copycats that are still going strong two decades after its invention. That influence was recognised once again at the 2026 World's 50 Best Restaurants ceremony, where Ferran Adrià received the Icon Award for his contribution to modern gastronomy. Although El Bulli closed in 2011, Adrià continues his work through the El Bulli Foundation, a non-profit organisation dedicated to culinary research and education. While it may seem that Spain quietly took over the top of the rankings once again in 2026, the truth is the rise of Spanish cuisine is a perfect storm of sorts. Avant-garde Spanish cuisine began long before Adrià started making headlines at El Bulli. The nueva cocina vasca – new Basque cuisine – was started by a group of friends in San Sebastián in the 1970s. Chefs including Juan Mari Arzak, who won the Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2011 50 Best, and Pedro Subijana of Akelarre, pulled together under a new flag that combined Basque tradition and reverence for product with creativity and innovation. This put Spain on the global haute cuisine map, inspiring a generation of chefs, including Adrià, and the rising tide has carried chefs across the country to the top of world cuisine. Beyond the shiny kitchens of Spain’s starred spots, however, lies the real richness of Spanish cuisine – the incredible ingredients. Spain provides the world with olive oil, wines, cheeses, seafood, fruits and vegetables, but it makes sure to save the best for its own tables. Spain’s vast diversity also plays an instrumental role in its culinary dominance. Across Spain's 50 provinces, knowledge runs deep when it comes to the cultivation and cooking of traditional ingredients – everything from the prawns of Cataluña to the baby tear-shaped peas of Basque Country to the red tuna of Andalucía to cave-aged blue cheeses of Asturias. A record 96.8 million international tourists visited Spain in 2025, more than 25 per cent of whom took part in food- and wine-related activities during their stay. This is in part thanks to the accessibility of the best of Spanish cuisine, which is a high-low, intensely joyful mélange of experiences. Even Spain’s signature small bites, pintxos and tapas, often use techniques pioneered by top chefs, from foams to spherifications. “The way of eating in Spain is a privilege,” says León. “We have both fine dining restaurants and affordable tapas, not to mention excellent mid-range restaurants – 20-40 euros per person – that you can’t find in other countries.” León is right – the Michelin Guide Spain & Andorra 2026 recognises 204 Bib Gourmand restaurants for offering good-quality food at affordable prices. Local culture, whether you are on the beaches of Cádiz or the cliffs of Galicia, always goes hand in hand with food. From vibrant food markets to neighbourhood tapas bars, everyday eating in Spain is a celebration of product. Spanish chefs have reached the peak once again, and with role models like Adrià, Arzak and more, there’s no shortage of inspiration. Spain’s top players are thrillingly diverse – on one hand, restaurants like DiverXO and Disfrutar focus on fusing culinary art and science, while restaurants like Etxebarri, Elkano, and Quique Dacosta are temples to high-quality ingredients. The future of Spanish cuisine will depend not only on wild innovation but also on the sustainability of high-quality ingredients and the close link to tradition – but for now, Spain may just be the foodiest country in Europe.

item.title: Appalachian Trail Threatened by ‘Uncommonly’ Large Wildfire in White Mountains
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
A wildfire that may be the largest in White Mountains history is currently burning just miles from the Appalachian Trail, and officials say a human may have caused it. The Wild River Fire started on Tuesday, November 3, in Coos County, New Hampshire, and has grown to 865 acres as of this writing, with just 11 percent contained. While the Appalachian Trail (AT), roughly 10 miles from the blaze, currently remains open, the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) has closed numerous other trails and roads in the area. Small brush fires and wildfires occur in White Mountains National Forest (WMNF) almost every year, but according to Gorham Fire Chief Philip Cloutier, who spoke with NHPR on Wednesday, a wildfire of this size is unusual. Both extended drought and extremely dry fall conditions have fuelled its speedy growth. “That’s very uncommon in our area,” Cloutier said. “The largest wildfire that we can remember was just under 100 acres, and that was over 20 years ago.” Officially, USFS is still investigating the wildfire’s source. Authorities have indicated that they believe it was human-caused, though they have released no further details about the origin. While the Wild River Fire is burning roughly 10 miles east of the AT, no closures or evacuations have been issued for the trail yet. Still, other trails in the area (some of which connect with the AT) have been closed. Below is the USFS list of trail closures in WMNF. We will update this article if more closures are announced. In addition to these closures, Wild River Road is also closed in its entirety. According to the USFS, the response to the Wild River Fire has been swift, and additional resources, including thje Cherokee Hotshot Crew and a smoke suppression module, have been sent to aid in the fight. The area’s steep, rocky terrain, remote location, and wet conditions have made it particularly challenging for firefighters. A USFS spokesperson told NHPR that firefighters had to cross the Wild River on foot to mount a direct attack. However, the efforts seem to be paying off. On November 4, the fire swelled to 982 acres. That evening, it was reduced to 865 acres, where it remains currently. “I am proud of the firefighters who responded quickly and continue to work tirelessly to contain the Wild River Fire,” noted Josh Sjostrom, District Ranger for the White Mountain National Forest’s Androscoggin Ranger District. “We will continue to work with our neighbors and local and state partners to contain this fire.”

item.title: Only one London restaurant made the World’s 50 Best list – but there is a secret second hiding in plain sight
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Well, well, well, it’s that time of year again. Last night, the crème de la crème of the world’s fine-dining scene gathered in Lima, Peru, to celebrate the latest iteration of The 50 Best Restaurants in the World – formerly known as The World’s 50 Best – awards. Usually, London secures between two and four spots on the prestigious list, which guides those looking to experience some of the world's most progressive food. But to say that it hasn't been a particularly good year for the capital of the UK would be an understatement. In fact, it’s the city’s worst year on record. At the ceremony in Lima, Peru, on Wednesday 4 November, only one restaurant from the British capital made the top 50. Ikoyi, the two-Michelin-starred restaurant from chef Jeremy Chan and co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, landed at number 48. They previously won last year's Highest Climber Award, reaching position 15. Founded in 2017 by childhood friends Chan and Hassan-Odukale, the restaurant has risen to global acclaim for crafting flavours and textures so imaginative that they’re difficult to categorise. Housed in a copper-clad dining room at 180 Strand, it serves tasting menus that utilise rare and lesser-known spices from across Africa and Asia alongside the finest, meticulously sourced British ingredients. Chan’s richly layered dishes resist conventional culinary labels, and chop and change with the seasons, though you could come across well-loved hits such as succulent, delicately grilled turbot with egusi miso, tender, flame-licked Nigerian-inspired suya with creamed peas, or Chan's signature silken lobster head smoked jollof rice. Ikoyi's inclusion in the list over the years has had a tangible impact on the business. "It has had a very positive impact on the restaurant and the business," Hassan-Odukale tells Condé Nast Traveller. "Last year, in particular, we were 15th on the list, and there was a spike in bookings. We were generally busier in the year following the announcement than before it." According to the co-founder, the recognition has also helped the restaurant attract talent, both in the kitchen and front of house. But Ikoyi isn't London's only connection to this year's top 50 list. Sitting 20 places above it, at number 28, is Trèsind Studio, the trailblazing Indian restaurant in Dubai that became the first Indian restaurant in the world to receive three Michelin stars in 2025. Helmed by chef Himanshu Saini, the intimate 20-seater dining room on Palm Jumeirah is known for its boundary-pushing interpretation of Indian cuisine, with a flamboyant tasting menu that spotlights the huge country's extraordinary and still relatively unsung regional diversity. In May 2026, the restaurant group behind Trèsind Studio made its London debut, opening the sultry Trèsind Mayfair on Hanover Street, just a hop, skip and a jump from Oxford Circus. While London's Trèsind is not a replica of the three-Michelin-starred Trèsind Studio, much of the menu is cherry-picked from the Dubai original, with Saini overseeing what comes out of the kitchen, helmed by executive chef Amit Bagyal. The restaurant’s dodgy, mid-2000s website is a smokescreen for what is truly a sophisticated, charming and delicious restaurant experience. Like the original, Bagyal’s tasting menu is designed to take diners on a romp through India's regions, reimagining traditional dishes with the help of contemporary techniques and unexpected ingredient combinations. At £138, the vibrant, invigorating tasting menu is worthy of wiping your calendar for. Dishes transplanted from the original include the theatrical Khichdi of India, a comforting, porridge-like rice-and-lentil dish celebrating ingredients from across the country's states, which are presented on a map. There is also Saini’s soul-soothing umami mushroom chai with intriguing truffle milk powder, and Bengali kosha mangsho, a rich, slow-braised mutton curry. For those reluctant to commit to an all-out tasting menu, there's also a £42 lunch and a shorter £75 tasting menu. Downstairs, meanwhile, cocktail bar Tryst uses Indian ingredients and regional flavours to conjure an array of inventive drinks. Of course, the success or failure of an entire city's restaurant scene can’t be measured by a single awards ceremony. The 50 Best rankings are compiled from the votes of around 1,100 international restaurant industry insiders, and inevitably reflect where those voters have travelled and eaten over the preceding 18 months. And while the awards tend to spotlight more rigid, exacting destination restaurants, some of London's most exciting cooking is happening in restaurants that don’t adhere to the traditional fine dining mould. "I guess if I had to look for some light in London's dining scene today, it would be the rise of more upmarket casual restaurants like Mountain and Impala," says Hassan-Odukale. "It's great to have access to good cooking, ingredient sourcing and hospitality without the fine dining price tag. Definitely a good thing for Londoners." And who are we to argue with that?

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off. Making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following. Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack. - Total Time 1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling) Need to make a substitution? - CakeStep 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking). Step 2Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan. Step 3Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil. Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature. - MousseStep 4Place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes. Step 5Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute. Step 6Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth. Step 7Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more. Step 8Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours. - Ganache and AssemblyStep 9Place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes. Step 10Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells). Step 11To serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

item.title: The Canadian province where swear words are sacred
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Excuse my French? The swear words that used to be illegal in Canada Quebec has perfected such a vast variety of profanity that it's been called "the Amazon rainforest of swear words". But uttering these blasphemous terms could have once landed you in prison. Thursday nights at Quebec City jazz joint Bar Sainte-Angèle are known for a buzzy open mic where veterans swap improvisational riffs with students from the nearby music conservatory. But as I elbowed towards the bar on a recent evening, I overheard a patron practicing a different local art with equal parts precision and heart. "Sacrement d'ostie de tabarnak", he said, cursing as his eyebrows climbed towards the bar's heavy-timbered ceiling. Taken literally, it translates to "sacrament of the communion host of the tabernacle". But the real meaning is anything but churchly. Warning: Some readers may find language in this story offensive. Speakers of Québécois French are known for using a unique class of blasphemous swear words derived from Catholic terms known as sacres ("sacred" profanities). Among the most famous are the seemingly innocent tabarnak ("tabernacle"), câlisse ("chalice") and Criss ("Christ"). But when angrily deployed, they carry all the offensive heft of English profanity. Yelling "tabarnak!" is just as off-colour as the English F-word, while letting out a "câlisse!" is something closer to "damn". And they don't stop there. When researching his 1980 book Le Guide Raisonné des Jurons (The Reasoned Guide to Swear Words), local folklorist Jean-Pierre Pichette recorded some 1,800 Québécois sacres. Some linguists now put the number at closer to 2,000. It's a lexicon of such variety, scope and colour that one expert compares the province's range of profanity to a biodiversity hotspot. "It's like the Amazon rainforest of swear words," says Jean-François Joubert, an instructor at Quebec City's Cégep Garneau and author of Le Sacre du Québec (The Profanity of Quebec). When I met Joubert for locally brewed beers in Quebec City's working-class Limoilou neighbourhood, he gestured over my shoulder at a patron sitting nearby. "Did you hear that?" he whispered. I didn't. "An excellent string of sacres", he said, with the smile of a lifelong connoisseur. Some are biblical or liturgical deep cuts, such as simonaque (a reference to religious profiteering, and a slightly milder curse than tabarnak or câlisse) and ciboire (the sacred vessel used to hold the Eucharist, and another mid-tier swear). Not all sacres are so arcane. Sainte vierge déculottée and sainte vierge en bicycle evoke the Virgin Mary appearing bare-bottomed, or on a bicycle, respectively. Asked about his personal favourites, Joubert offered the emphatically NSFW ostie consacrée au cul de cochon, or "consecrated communion host in a pig's ass". Travellers to Quebec are likely to hear plenty of sacres in jazz bars, at hockey games and on street corners. Souvenir shops in Quebec City and Montreal sell shirts printed with phrases like "Je m'en câlisse, a vulgar way to say "I don’t care". At Musée POP in the city of Trois-Rivières, there are curses emblasoned on the wall of an ongoing exhibit exploring Québécois popular culture – a curatorial choice hinting that sacres go beyond the usual hammer-hits-thumb exclamations. "They're so much a part of our life", says Michelle Bélanger, the museum's general director. "Sacres are a very important part of our history, culture, and identity." What's more, understanding them sheds light on a side of Quebec that most visitors overlook entirely: a foul-mouthed legacy of cultural resistance. It's hard to pinpoint the origin of sacres because, until relatively recently, even the most prolific cursers didn't write them down. Blasphemy was illegal in New France, the territory founded by the French in the 16th Century. In the early days, it was taken seriously. A first offence came with a hefty fine, writes Pichette; a third offence could put you in prison for a month. That doesn't mean early French-speaking settlers held back. Joubert traces sacres to immigrants arriving from French cities like Rouen and La Rochelle that were historically Protestant but whose populations had undergone forced conversions to Catholicism. "Even though on paper they're Catholic, they come from regions that had strife and religious conflict," he says. Joubert notes religious orders were a prominent part of life in New France, and thinks early settlers must have chafed at their presence. Blasphemy was a way to subvert the Church's power. "If you look at the words, they're mainly about the Mass, like the classic ostie, câlisse and tabarnak," Joubert says. "They were taking some of the mystery, or mystique, away from the Mass." Not all historians agree with Joubert's origin story. But there's a widespread consensus that Quebec's propensity for profanity was supercharged by a series of events in the 19th Century. In 1837 and 1838, British forces quelled two armed uprisings by largely secular, French-speaking nationalists. Following those rebellions, the Catholic Church stepped in, becoming the rigidly conservative administrators of everything from education to healthcare. "Starting in the 1840s, [Catholicism] became omnipresent in nearly every aspect of public life", says Québécois historian René Hardy, a professor emeritus at the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières. Resistance to the change sparked an upwelling of profanity that Hardy has examined through the Church's own writings. "When the bishops' council met in 1886, they concurred that using sacres had become the cardinal sin of all French Canadians," he says. Then, in the 1960s, many Québécois rejected the Church's heavy-handed presence in a social upheaval that became known as the Quiet Revolution. The province rapidly secularised. At the same time, sacres became a way for Quebec's French speakers to bond, reaffirming a language and culture that could feel marginalised – both by a majority anglophone country and the broader francophone world, says Yulia Bosworth, an associate professor of linguistics at Binghamton University specialising in Quebec French. "The religious meaning is lost, but in the 1960s these terms acquired a countercultural significance that still remains," Bosworth says. "Today, sacres are probably the most emblematic and recognisable element of Quebec's linguistic identity." For linguists like Bosworth, it's not the religious source of Québécois sacres that's unusual. After all, most profanity worldwide falls into three broad categories: sexual terms, words related to bodily excretions and religious expressions. But the sheer scale of these "sacred" curse words stands out. "With [roughly] 7,000 world languages, I'd put Quebec French in the top 25 – maybe top 10", in terms of the variety of curse words, Bosworth says. The words are also unusually adaptable, inviting innovation. Many sacres can be variously used as nouns, adjectives, verbs and adverbs, an elasticity displayed in a famous cursing scene from the bilingual Canadian action-comedy Bon Cop, Bad Cop. "English is capable of this kind of creativity, with the F-word and others, but the degree to which Quebec French has taken it is absolutely remarkable," Bosworth says. Sacres can also be linked together to form compound curses, which Montreal-based actor and YouTuber Nir Guzinski likens to assembling Ikea furniture. To illustrate the process, he offered the salty tirade "esti de câlisse de tabarnak de maudit de Criss" (literally: "communion host of chalice of tabernacle of cursed of Christ"). An online Québécois swear generator creates paragraph-long curses that are a modern blasphemer's masterclass. Given the colourful vocabulary on hand, it's unsurprising that many French-language learners visiting or living in Quebec are eager to experiment with sacres. "If you're interested in French-Canadian culture, you'll encounter them everywhere," says Frédéric Patenaude, a Montreal-based language teacher who hosts the Quebec French Podcast and is the author of Quebec French for Beginners. He teaches the sacres in class but advises caution when deploying them. "It's subtle. Swear words are always tricky when you learn a second language because it's a question of the situation, the level of formality," he says, explaining that a common misconception is that sacres are "cute". "Yes, you can use them everywhere, but they do sound like swear words to us," he says. For those dipping a toe in, he recommends trying out the milder versions that modify basic sacres – much as English-language speakers might say "darn" or "fudge" in place of spicier curses. Instead of saying "tabarnak", he says to opt for "tabarnouche", "tabarouette" or "tabarslack" – words that get the idea across with less risk of causing offence. "If you're a tourist and start saying 'tabarnak' to everyone, this will not work for you," agrees Joubert. But he is enthusiastic about the prospect of newcomers and visitors dabbling in some light blasphemy. He thinks that, like generations of Quebecois, they might even find a way to build social bonds through profanity. "If you get the right person, it's a great way of actually participating," he says. "It's a great road into the culture." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: REVIEW: The new London restaurants to try in November 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in November 2026 Following the devastating fire that destroyed beloved Endo at the Rotunda in September 2025, a hole has been left in London’s dining scene ever since. So, when news of Endo Chelsea broke, it may come as no surprise that securing one of the 10 seats in the intimate omakase felt akin to getting your hands on Glastonbury tickets. The new West London outpost is darker and sexier yet distinctly more traditional than its predecessor at the Rotunda. Inspired by the sushi counters of the 1920s and 30s, the atmosphere is theatrical and practically electric as we wait for the star of the show to appear. I take my seat, sip my delicious tea-infused Negroni, and watch as the seamlessly choreographed 19-course performance unfolds. Undoubtedly, Endo is the star of this show, handing each guest a piece of sushi and swapping tales at the same time. From the beautifully ornate sake cups, designed and handcrafted by Endo himself, to the three varieties of rice used throughout the omakase, each paying homage to one of his great teachers. The food is, unsurprisingly, exceptional. Local produce meets Japanese technique. Much of tonight’s fish comes from Cornwall, where Endo recently lived and worked alongside local fishermen. Highlights include langoustine nigiri, turbot and mackerel, alongside an oyster paired with a cup of exceptional 200-year-old discontinued sake. Then there’s the Wagyu with cep mushroom and chive. Three hours slip past in the blink of an eye. A triumphant new chapter, this new opening is like a phoenix rising from the ashes. Welcome to the new church of Endo. Lucy Bruton Address: 8-9 Blacklands Terrace, London SW3 2SP This isn’t just a new restaurant to try in London, Lunette is the new restaurant in London. The debut solo restaurant of chef Florence Knight, previously of Sessions Art Club and Polpetto, has all the hallmarks of an A-list haunt. There’s the swishy address – squirrelled down a 10th-floor corridor and up some glossy stairs within St. Clement, the first hotel from Soho House founder Nick Jones since he stepped back from the private members’ club. There’s design-showroom good looks in the long dining room with purposefully incongruous tables: steel rectangles, glossy round tables and a cream sofa seating area in the middle for the truly brave. And then of course, the million-pound Thames views with an outdoor terrace that is destined to have its own waitlist come summer. Rare for these seen-and-be-seen spots, though, the food is actually great. So phenomenal, in fact, I found myself scraping every last morsel and sliver of sauce from each plate. The four-course lunch and six-course supper menu is plainly worded but is anything but. Runner bean, squid and yarrow translates to a bright green bowl of fresh herby magic. Equally dazzling is the marigold orange of the cock crab, pepper and yolk, a lick-the-plate-clean egg-jammy, buttery risotto with a footnote of peppery heat. I was sceptical of the custard, onion and caviar, with the latter ingredient often used so haphazardly that it lost all appeal. This is where Knight’s restraint really shines – the caviar is respectfully the star rather than a hedonistic afterthought. There’s a masterful light and shade with each dish, along with the option for wine pairings to really hit the high notes. If you go it alone, most bottles of wine are under £100, which is refreshing. Likewise, the £16 signature martini is poured in two servings into the daintiest glasses. With two pudding courses, I left full, happy and wondering how long it will take until a Michelin star comes calling. Lauren Burvill Address: 180, The Thames, 12 Temple Place, Temple, London WC2R 2NF I must admit, I never thought a hole-in-the-wall this charming could exist a few steps from London’s chaotic Strand. But on a gloomy work night, when I walked into this new bistro housed in an old church furniture workshop, it felt like the place had been here for decades. The comfort food here is straight out of a French farmhouse, with a subtle British touch. It’s all bursting with flavour, with portions large enough to satisfy you, while leaving room for the next course. We start off our evening with a one-bite raw beef croustade dusted with comté and, because I can never get enough of my favourite French cheese, moved on to a tarragon-topped comté quiche that I know will become a post-work staple. The mains are French classics that weave in local fare (think stuffed cabbage chou farci but with pigeon); we opt for delectable grilled mackerel in a rich lobster bisque, and what might officially be one of my top three comfort dishes in London: the hen of the woods (a sponge-sized nutty mushroom that grows around oak trees) and armagnac vol-au-vent with sauce Parisienne. I grew up with my mother making vol-au-vent, so enjoying a forest-y twist on such a nostalgic dish was a treat. For dessert we shared an unbeatable chocolate mousse drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with flaky salt, and one of my favourite French desserts: black fig clafoutis. For those unfamiliar, this eggy, crustless tart typically uses whole cherries, so not having to worry about the pits with this version was a win-win. Tamara Southward Address: 42 Maiden Lane, Covent Garden, WC2E 7LJ It’s not often I find myself dining at the same restaurant twice in one week, but The Horses is such a hot ticket right now that it’s no surprise when one of my more switched-on foodie friends excitedly tells me that she’s booked us lunch there a few days after my first visit. And I have no problem returning – this latest outpost from Public House Group (The Hart in Marylebone, The Pelican in Notting Hill) hits all their signatures: top-drawer UK produce, served simply and beautifully, in an elevated homage to the great British pub. The Horses dates back to 1790, and has been revamped by PHC with a traditional pub on the ground floor and three levels of seafood dining on top, a nod to the former Smithfield fish market nearby. Downstairs is heaving when we arrive on Friday night, but escaping up a back staircase we enter into the relative calm of the dinky oyster bar. There’s a subtle sea theme running through the design, with limewashed ceilings, soft curtains reminiscent of sails or netting, orb lights hung with chains, and an ice-packed treasure chest of crustaceans overseeing it all from the horseshoe-shaped counter bar. It’s candlelit, intimate and wonderfully romantic. The chatty staff have a genuine enthusiasm for seafood – we get tips on which order to eat the oysters, freshly shucked in front of us, and whether they need a drop of homemade chilli sauce or mignonette. The cod’s roe on smoked bread is basically fancy taramasalata on toast and a fantastic pub snack, but the standout starters are the clams and cockles in a creamy, cider-y broth and the moreish squid coated in fried pastry crumbs with chilli mayo. Among the mains, the fish is the thing – there are six to choose from, plus specials, and six sauces to mix and match (“they’re actually all free right now, so I’d just go mad,” murmurs our waitress). Monkfish with langoustine gravy is satisfyingly meaty, and John Dory with the surprising recommendation of peppercorn sauce really works; but the star is the Dover Sole with garlic butter, accompanied by a pile of new potatoes studded generously with garlic, and sea greens. It all feels special but not stiffly formal, and I’ll be back yet again for pub snacks and pints in the near future. Olivia Squire As a Notting Hill resident with the luck of a job that’s given me dibs on newly opened restaurants, being at the centre of the anticipation is always exciting. But the lead-up to Nakimushi opening its doors felt quieter, as if those who’d caught a glimpse wanted to keep the place a secret immediately. On the affordable end compared to its sister restaurant Eel, Nakimushi is the marriage of Urchin and Robin’s Ramen – two former London residencies that now see chefs Yuji Shimokawa and Robin Kosuge bring opposite ends of Japanese cuisine together. We share wild hamachi with nori oil, vegetable ohitashi worth it for the mushrooms alone, and a tuna summer roll with blackberry and hibiscus (my favourite). For our mains, we choose lobster ramen with sobrassada and pistachio matcha ramen with daikon cress. If the veggie broth at a restaurant is this decadent (not to mention, healing), it’s a winner in my opinion. The ground floor is communal-style, where you watch your food being prepped in an open kitchen from counter seating or a shared table. But weave up the Scandi-style stairwell and you’re in a proper dining room, whose timber walls are covered with cool contemporary art and bottles of Japanese whisky. There’s only one dessert on the menu, the mugi-cha creme caramel; the only area I’d like to see revisited. It’s good, but perhaps not enough to warrant single status. Tamara Southward Romy Gill has been a permanent fixture on the London food scene for more than a decade. Since the unfortunate 2019 closure of her first restaurant, Romy’s Kitchen, in South Gloucestershire, Romy has become a welcome sight on TV screens between the release of three cookbooks – the latest being Romy Gill's India: Recipes from Home, in 2024. Being such a household name, you’d be forgiven for being surprised that her new venture, Romy Gill at The Pem, is the chef’s first restaurant in six years. It’s the aforementioned cookbook that greets us as we pass over the threshold, after weaving through Conrad London St. James, into a fantastically crimson dining space. Privacy panels divide the restaurant's heart into booth hideouts that feel more intimate than the sprawling space they’re set in, while tables along each side offer corners where besotted foodies feast under subdued lamplight. Cocktails arrive, the taste of cumin curiously coating my palate as I sip on the Malhar, crafted with Amrut Single Malt and homemade cumin syrup – the Anarkali isn’t to my taste, but a Negroni obsessive’s dream, I’m sure. Starters land and the feast begins as we pluck decoratively presented king prawns (and king they are) from their heads and savour melt-in-the-mouth tandoori lamb chops. The highlight, however, is the samosa chaat; a crisp samosa topped with chickpeas, sev, pomegranate seeds and yoghurt in a sensational jumble of taste and texture that we long to do all over again. Heaps of rice and chunks of torn naan, fresh out of the charcoal tandoor, come into action, soaking up the sweet butter chicken sauce before our waiter performatively surrounds the hake moilee in a refreshing, vibrant curry leaf broth. After initial insistence that we need no dessert, we cave and coat sugar-dusted churros in a decadent chocolate sauce – a perfectly gluttonous finish, after all, to a warming meal that ushers us gently into the autumn months. Connor Sturges Address: Romy Gill at The Pem, 22-28 Broadway, London SW1H 0BH Best new London restaurants in September 2026 There’s something ever so cool about anonymity, and as I walked straight past the door of Kid in Soho, I had to remind myself of this. There are no signs, bells or whistles here, just a rusty brown door with an almost imperceptible goat symbol marked on it. Kid holds a quiet, understated vibe that oozes confidence – and rightly so. The hotly anticipated restaurant is the latest project from former Mangal II chef Sertaç Dirik, who’s teamed up with David Carter of London mainstays Oma, Agora and Smokestak, making it quite the force to be reckoned with. Inside, the vibe is dimly lit, with exposed brick and a bustling open kitchen, reaching far beyond what the subtle exterior might at first suggest. The menu, meanwhile, is Turkish-inspired but with plenty of twists, blending a lovely mix of soul-soothing, comforting classics with an elevated execution. Highlights included the balloon-like tombik pide (worth visiting for alone), a smoked aubergine dip topped with whisker-thin grains, and the İçli Köfte – the most sumptuous ball of dry-aged beef, juicy and flavoursome, that will be living in my mind rent-free for a while. Of course, most customers opt for the namesake shoulder of goat on the menu, served in a huge traditional clay pot and slow-cooked overnight for the ultimate fall-away meat. Interestingly, the wine list is ordered not just by region, but by when wine-making practices first began in each destination. We opted for a light Cypriot glass to match the restaurant's tone and offset some of the richer dishes. So, is the new kid on the block actually worth the hype? I’d say yes – and I’d even hazard a guess that this new dining address has some seriously long-standing appeal. Lucy Bruton Address: Kid, 53-55 Frith Street, London W1D 4SJ One could be forgiven for thinking this rather enviable London postcode – on W1S’s Cork Street – can be a little pretentious at times. But that’s certainly not the case at Bar Finch. Perusing the menu prior to arrival, I felt – dare I say – a touch underwhelmed. Burgers and chips, Caesar salad, roast chicken; you know the drill. But that’s not the case either. What you actually get when you patter down the steps is a new, polished neighbourhood go-to that feels akin to plopping yourself down in a very chic living room, complete with terribly friendly staff and the cheerful spirit of a proper Italian bacaro. Ashy wood panelling and lashings of texture keep things cosy, while great slabs of marble wherever you look remind you that you’re still firmly in Mayfair. Suitably settled in our plush leather booth, we got stuck in. The menu, a triumph of Italian-tinged comfort food, now makes sense. Portion sizes are perfect for sharing (and actually so – not just billed that way on the menu only to arrive disappointingly tiny). The hand-rolled pastas were most popular among fellow diners, arriving tossed in silky, slow-cooked ragù, while a tomato salad and a side of beans tasted as fresh as anything you’ll eat all week. The steak has a delightfully indulgent thread of marbling that rivals the tabletops, and proper crispy chips, but the dish to order is the chicken piccata – complete with a salty, crackling skin curled up pleasingly at the edges and a generous smattering of oily capers for good measure. Drinks pairings are treated with equal flair. There’s a curated wine list featuring both indie Italian winemakers and classic European vintages, but you won’t feel shortchanged if you skip them all and go straight for the cocktails, which are far too good to miss. All the Italian classics are present, but the standout – promptly earning a second order – was the Champs-Élysées; bright with lemon and Green Chartreuse, given a grown-up edge with a hit of cognac. Whatever you do, don’t leave without ordering the tiramisu, which is utterly huge (so don’t say you weren’t warned). Make sure to leave room, as taking leftovers home isn’t allowed. But who cares, in any case? This is a delightful spot to hunker down on a cold and gloomy evening at leisure. There’s no need to rush away so soon. Charley Ward At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market. Following the closure of The Water House Project in June, their new home is an impeccably designed space, flowing from raised beds outside, where the chefs pick fresh herbs, into a bar area with stainless steel countertops and handcrafted oak furniture, and through to the dining room, which serves 24 covers in an intimate nightly sitting. The food measures up to the space. Chef Gabriel draws on his Northumberland upbringing and the region’s traditional cooking techniques, while adding a playful touch with in-house ingredients such as miso, koji and garums. Start with a punchy, syrupy fig leaf martini at the bar before embarking on the 11-course tasting menu. The ensemble hits a high note immediately with a rich, comforting cep and Madeira tea, before moving into bites that challenge the palate while remaining comforting and, ultimately, delicious. The courses balance refreshing zing, like the oyster with cucumber and sorrel, with familiar but elevated mouthfuls, like the moreish onion crumpet. Larger plates, including a smoked haddock porridge (oyster mushroom for vegetarians), hit a hearty note. The meal ended on singing hinnies, a traditional griddle cake, with boozy-forward lavender and Laphroaig cream. If you manage to have some room left, the seasonal cheese selection isn’t to be missed. This is a savoury, umami-rich tasting menu that has immediately risen to the top of my list for celebratory meals. The team have nailed the difficult task of creating fine-dining plates without a stuffy atmosphere. Gabriel and Patricia’s history of supper clubs, where their journey began, can still be felt in the environment they’ve curated at Waterhouse. Chloe Laws Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack.
